did_you_know.text: The title identifies the psalm as “For the choir director. A psalm of David,” including both the term “For the choir director” and the name David.
From the very beginning, the king is described as rejoicing not only in the Lord’s strength but also in his salvation; his joy is therefore connected to divine deliverance.
The verse presents two forms of petition: “the desire of his heart” and “the request of his lips.” The Lord is described as granting the king what he asks for and not withholding his prayer.
The blessings are described as going before the king, and he also receives “a crown of pure gold”—reflecting the biblical meaning of the word “pure gold.”
The king asked for life, and the verse emphasizes that the Lord granted it to him. It also mentions “length of days, forever and ever,” intensifying the idea of long life.
Salvation is not described merely as practical deliverance; it also grants the king honor, majesty, and splendor. Thus, the psalm connects salvation with dignified royal status.
The verse explains the king’s stability through two foundations: his trust in the Lord and the steadfast love of the Most High. Therefore, it says of him, “he will not be shaken.”
At this point, the focus of the psalm shifts: from describing the king’s blessings, it moves to his confrontation with his enemies, using images of the hand, the right hand, and royal power.
Even when the enemies devise a plot, the text emphasizes its failure: they may plan evil, but they cannot carry out their scheme.
The conclusion shifts to the plural form—“we will sing and praise.” After describing the king’s salvation and victory, the entire community is called to sing and praise the Lord’s might.
